claim: RNAi against hoe-1 attenuates hsp-6p::GFP induction in nuo-6(qm200) animals.
source: Knockdown of hoe-1 by RNAi is sufficient to attenuate UPRmt reporter activation induced by a loss-of-function mutation in the mitochondrial electron transport chain (ETC) complex I subunit NUO-6 (nuo-6(qm200)) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B, demonstrating reduced fluorescence intensity in hoe-1 RNAi treated animals.

claim: hoe-1 null mutants do not develop past late larval stage 3.
source: The hoe-1 null mutants do not develop past late larval stage 3, thus the allele is maintained over a balancer chromosome, tmC25 (Dejima et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation of developmental arrest in hoe-1 null animals.

claim: UPRmt induced by knockdown of spg-7 is robustly attenuated in hoe-1 null animals.
source: UPRmt induced by the knockdown of both the mitochondrial protease, spg-7, and ETC complex IV subunit, cco-1, is robustly attenuated in hoe-1 null animals (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E demonstrating reduced hsp-6p::GFP fluorescence in hoe-1(-/-) animals on spg-7 RNAi.

claim: UPRmt induced by knockdown of cco-1 is robustly attenuated in hoe-1 null animals.
source: UPRmt induced by the knockdown of both the mitochondrial protease, spg-7, and ETC complex IV subunit, cco-1, is robustly attenuated in hoe-1 null animals (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E demonstrating reduced hsp-6p::GFP fluorescence in hoe-1(-/-) animals on cco-1 RNAi.

claim: UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) is attenuated in hoe-1 null animals.
source: Furthermore, UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) is attenuated in hoe-1 null animals similarly to what is seen in nuo-6(qm200) animals on hoe-1 RNAi (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G demonstrating reduced hsp-6p::GFP fluorescence in nuo-6(qm200);hoe-1(-/-) animals.

claim: HOE-1 is generally required for maximal UPRmt activation.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that HOE-1 is generally required for maximal UPRmt activation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing attenuation of UPRmt under various stress conditions when hoe-1 is compromised.

claim: HOE-1 is predicted to localize to both nuclei and mitochondria.
source: HOE-1 is predicted to localize to both nuclei and mitochondria and this dual-localization has been shown for HOE-1 orthologs in Drosophila, mice, and human cell lines (Dubrovsky et al., 2004; Brzezniak et al., 2011; Rossmanith, 2011; Siira et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in other organisms and prediction for C. elegans HOE-1.

claim: HOE-1 orthologs in Drosophila, mice, and human cell lines show dual-localization to nuclei and mitochondria.
source: HOE-1 is predicted to localize to both nuclei and mitochondria and this dual-localization has been shown for HOE-1 orthologs in Drosophila, mice, and human cell lines (Dubrovsky et al., 2004; Brzezniak et al., 2011; Rossmanith, 2011; Siira et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: hoe-1::GFP homozygous animals grow and develop indistinguishably from wildtype animals.
source: Both hoe-1::GFP homozygous and hoe-1::GFP/hoe-1(-/-) trans-heterozygous animals grow and develop indistinguishably from wildtype animals suggesting that GFP-tagging HOE-1 does not compromise its essential functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: hoe-1::GFP/hoe-1(-/-) trans-heterozygous animals grow and develop indistinguishably from wildtype animals.
source: Both hoe-1::GFP homozygous and hoe-1::GFP/hoe-1(-/-) trans-heterozygous animals grow and develop indistinguishably from wildtype animals suggesting that GFP-tagging HOE-1 does not compromise its essential functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP-tagging HOE-1 does not compromise its essential functions.
source: Both hoe-1::GFP homozygous and hoe-1::GFP/hoe-1(-/-) trans-heterozygous animals grow and develop indistinguishably from wildtype animals suggesting that GFP-tagging HOE-1 does not compromise its essential functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GFP-tagged animals develop normally.

claim: HOE-1 localizes to both mitochondria and nuclei in C. elegans.
source: We found that HOE-1 localizes to both mitochondria and nuclei (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating co-localization with TMRE (mitochondria) and nuclear localization.

claim: hoe-1 contains two functional start codons.
source: hoe-1 contains two functional start codons.
evidence: Stated as a fact based on sequence analysis.

claim: Translation beginning from the first start codon (M1) produces a protein containing a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS).
source: Translation beginning from the first start codon (encoding methionine 1 (M1)) produces a protein containing a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and known protein targeting mechanisms.

claim: Translation beginning from the second start codon (M74) produces a nuclear specific protein.
source: Translation beginning from the second start codon (encoding methionine 74 (M74)), which is 3' to the MTS, produces a nuclear specific protein.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and protein targeting mechanisms.

claim: The feature of two functional start codons is conserved in human ELAC2.
source: This feature is conserved in human ELAC2 and it has been shown that mutating M1 to an alanine produces a mitochondrial-specific knockout (Brzezniak et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: Mutating M1 to alanine in human ELAC2 produces a mitochondrial-specific knockout.
source: This feature is conserved in human ELAC2 and it has been shown that mutating M1 to an alanine produces a mitochondrial-specific knockout (Brzezniak et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: The hoe-1(ΔMTS) mutation is sufficient to strongly attenuate mitochondrial targeting without impacting nuclear localization.
source: This mutation is sufficient to strongly attenuate mitochondrial targeting without impacting nuclear localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: UPRmt reporter activation by spg-7 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals.
source: UPRmt reporter activation by spg-7 and cco-1 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals (Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: UPRmt reporter activation by cco-1 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals.
source: UPRmt reporter activation by spg-7 and cco-1 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals (Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: UPRmt reporter activation is slightly elevated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals relative to wildtype.
source: In fact, UPRmt reporter activation is slightly elevated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals relative to wildtype.
evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Mitochondrial HOE-1 is not required for UPRmt activation.
source: These data suggest that mitochondrial HOE-1 is not required for UPRmt activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals do not show attenuated UPRmt.

claim: HOE-1 is predicted to contain two nuclear localization signals (NLS).
source: HOE-1 is predicted to contain two nuclear localization signals (NLS).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and prediction algorithms.

claim: hoe-1 null mutant animals are developmentally arrested.
source: Given that hoe-1 null mutant animals are developmentally arrested and hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals are superficially wildtype we reasoned that completely ablating nuclear localization of HOE-1 may result in recapitulation of the null phenotype.
evidence: Stated as an observation from earlier experiments.

claim: hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals are superficially wildtype.
source: Given that hoe-1 null mutant animals are developmentally arrested and hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals are superficially wildtype we reasoned that completely ablating nuclear localization of HOE-1 may result in recapitulation of the null phenotype.
evidence: Stated as an observation from earlier experiments.

claim: The hoe-1(ΔNLS) mutations are sufficient to strongly attenuate, but not completely ablate, HOE-1 nuclear localization whilst still allowing animals to develop to adulthood.
source: These mutations are sufficient to strongly attenuate, but not completely ablate, HOE-1 nuclear localization whilst still allowing animals to develop to adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-C.

claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 robustly attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by spg-7 RNAi.
source: In contrast to loss of mitochondrial HOE-1, loss of nuclear HOE-1 robustly attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by spg-7 RNAi (Figure 2E and F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by nuo-6(qm200).
source: and attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by nuo-6(qm200) (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target gene hsp-6 under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
source: Furthermore, loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target genes hsp-6 (Figure 2I) and cyp-14A1.4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A) under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target gene cyp-14A1.4 under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
source: Furthermore, loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target genes hsp-6 (Figure 2I) and cyp-14A1.4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A) under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claim: HOE-1 is required in the nucleus to facilitate UPRmt activation.
source: Together these data suggest that HOE-1 is required in the nucleus to facilitate UPRmt activation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing that nuclear, but not mitochondrial, HOE-1 is required for UPRmt.

claim: HOE-1 has both nuclear localization signals and a nuclear export signal (NES).
source: Like many nuclear localized proteins (la Cour et al., 2004), HOE-1 has both nuclear localization signals and a nuclear export signal (NES).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and citation to general knowledge about nuclear proteins.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals are superficially wildtype in their development but are sterile.
source: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals are superficially wildtype in their development but are sterile.
evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental characterization of the mutant.

claim: Homozygous hoe-1(ΔNES) animals have elevated nuclear HOE-1 accumulation relative to wildtype.
source: Homozygous hoe-1(ΔNES) animals have elevated nuclear HOE-1 accumulation relative to wildtype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C.

claim: The UPRmt reporter hsp-6p::GFP is robustly activated in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals similarly to that seen in nuo-6(qm200) and atfs-1(et15) mutant animals.
source: Strikingly, the UPRmt reporter hsp-6p::GFP is robustly activated in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals similarly to that seen in mitochondrial stressor nuo-6(qm200) and constitutive UPRmt activation in atfs-1 gain-of-function (atfs-1(et15)) mutant animals (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) mildly induces the UPRmt reporter hsp-60p::GFP.
source: hoe-1(ΔNES) also mildly induces the less sensitive UPRmt reporter hsp-60p::GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The UPRmt gene hsp-6 is upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: We found that the UPRmt genes encoding a chaperone protein (hsp-6), stress response involved C-type lectin (clec-47), and P450 enzyme (cyp-14A4.1) are all upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The UPRmt gene clec-47 is upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: We found that the UPRmt genes encoding a chaperone protein (hsp-6), stress response involved C-type lectin (clec-47), and P450 enzyme (cyp-14A4.1) are all upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The UPRmt gene cyp-14A4.1 is upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: We found that the UPRmt genes encoding a chaperone protein (hsp-6), stress response involved C-type lectin (clec-47), and P450 enzyme (cyp-14A4.1) are all upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3C, D and E).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: UPRmt activation is dependent upon the transcription factor ATFS-1.
source: UPRmt activation is dependent upon the transcription factor ATFS-1 (Haynes et al., 2010; Nargund et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Knockdown of atfs-1 is sufficient to completely attenuate UPRmt reporter activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: Knockdown of atfs-1 is sufficient to completely attenuate UPRmt reporter activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3F and G), showing that UPRmt induction by hoe-1(ΔNES) is ATFS-1 dependent.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: UPRmt induction by hoe-1(ΔNES) is ATFS-1 dependent.
source: Knockdown of atfs-1 is sufficient to completely attenuate UPRmt reporter activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3F and G), showing that UPRmt induction by hoe-1(ΔNES) is ATFS-1 dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that atfs-1 RNAi blocks hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNLS+ΔNES) animals have UPRmt reporter activation comparable to wildtype animals.
source: Indeed, hoe-1(ΔNLS+ΔNES) animals have UPRmt reporter activation comparable to wildtype animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: hoe-1(ΔMTS+ΔNES) animals have even higher activation of UPRmt than hoe-1(ΔNES) alone.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, hoe-1(ΔMTS+ΔNES) animals have even higher activation of UPRmt than hoe-1(ΔNES) alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) triggers UPRmt activation due to elevated nuclear HOE-1 levels.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that hoe-1(ΔNES) triggers UPRmt activation due to elevated nuclear HOE-1 levels.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that nuclear localization is required and that preventing nuclear export is sufficient for UPRmt activation.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals appear to have UPRmt activated specifically in the intestine.
source: Contrary to UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) and atfs-1(et15), hoe-1(ΔNES) animals appear to have UPRmt activated specifically in the intestine (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: UPRmt has been shown to be able to be signaled across tissues, particularly from neurons to intestine.
source: We questioned if this UPRmt activation is occurring cell autonomously or non-cell autonomously as UPRmt has been shown to be able to be signaled across tissues, particularly from neurons to intestine (Durieux et al., 2011; Berendzen et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only attenuated when HOE-1 is selectively degraded in the intestine.
source: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only attenuated when HOE-1 is selectively degraded in the intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B.

claim: Compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 activates UPRmt cell-autonomously in the intestine.
source: This data strongly suggests that compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 activates UPRmt cell-autonomously in the intestine.
evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific degradation experiments.

claim: The UPRER reporter hsp-4p::GFP is not activated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: We find that the UPRER reporter hsp-4p::GFP is not activated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that hoe-1(ΔNES) does not cause ER stress nor cellular proteotoxic stress.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) does not cause ER stress nor cellular proteotoxic stress.
source: We find that the UPRER reporter hsp-4p::GFP is not activated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that hoe-1(ΔNES) does not cause ER stress nor cellular proteotoxic stress.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of UPRER activation.

claim: The basal reporter ges-1p::GFPcyto is only mildly upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype.
source: Additionally, a basal reporter of GFP that has been used to proxy general protein expression (Gitschlag et al., 2016), ges-1p::GFPcyto, is only mildly upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claim: Impaired nuclear export of HOE-1 specifically activates UPRmt.
source: Together these findings support that impaired nuclear export of HOE-1 specifically activates UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of UPRER activation and minimal effect on general protein expression.

claim: UPRmt is known to be triggered when mitochondrial membrane potential is compromised.
source: UPRmt is known to be triggered when mitochondrial membrane potential is compromised (Rolland et al., 2019; Shpilka et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential is severely depleted in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: Consistent with UPRmt activation, we found that mitochondrial membrane potential is severely depleted in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals exhibit compromised mitochondrial membrane potential without UPRmt activation.
source: However, hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals also exhibit compromised mitochondrial membrane potential without UPRmt activation suggesting that decreased membrane potential does not guarantee UPRmt induction (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Decreased membrane potential does not guarantee UPRmt induction.
source: However, hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals also exhibit compromised mitochondrial membrane potential without UPRmt activation suggesting that decreased membrane potential does not guarantee UPRmt induction (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals have reduced membrane potential but no UPRmt activation.

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential is not rescued in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals on atfs-1 RNAi.
source: Mitochondrial membrane potential is not rescued in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals on atfs-1 RNAi (Figure 4C and D) suggesting that reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is not a result of UPRmt activation.
evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is not a result of UPRmt activation.
source: Mitochondrial membrane potential is not rescued in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals on atfs-1 RNAi (Figure 4C and D) suggesting that reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is not a result of UPRmt activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking UPRmt does not rescue membrane potential.

claim: Compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 results in depletion of mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Taken together, these data show that compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 results in depletion of mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data.

claim: Depletion in membrane potential correlates with UPRmt activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: Furthermore, this depletion in membrane potential correlates with UPRmt activation, consistent with the possibility that hoe-1(ΔNES) activates UPRmt via depletion of mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between reduced membrane potential and UPRmt activation.

claim: UPRmt activation is dependent upon nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor ATFS-1.
source: UPRmt activation is dependent upon nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor ATFS-1 (Nargund et al., 2012; Nargund et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Both hoe-1(ΔNES) and nuo-6(qm200) animals have elevated nuclear accumulation of ATFS-1 relative to wildtype.
source: Both hoe-1(ΔNES) and nuo-6(qm200) animals have elevated nuclear accumulation of ATFS-1 relative to wildtype (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: nuo-6(qm200) animals exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype.
source: However, while nuo-6(qm200) animals exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype, hoe-1(ΔNES) animals do not (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals do not exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype.
source: However, while nuo-6(qm200) animals exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype, hoe-1(ΔNES) animals do not (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: atfs-1 mRNA levels are elevated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype comparable to that seen in nuo-6(qm200) animals.
source: We find that atfs-1 mRNA levels are also elevated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype comparable to that seen in nuo-6(qm200) animals (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The transcription factor DVE-1 is required for full UPRmt activation.
source: The transcription factor DVE-1 is required for full UPRmt activation (Haynes et al., 2007; Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Accumulation of DVE-1::GFP in intestinal cell nuclei is significantly higher in hoe-1(ΔNES) than in wildtype animals.
source: We found that accumulation of DVE-1::GFP in intestinal cell nuclei is significantly higher in hoe-1(ΔNES) than in wildtype animals (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is a result of increased nuclear accumulation of UPRmt transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1.
source: Together, these data suggest that UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is a result of increased nuclear accumulation of UPRmt transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased nuclear levels of both transcription factors.

claim: The canonical role of HOE-1 is to cleave 3'-trailer sequences from nascent tRNAs.
source: The canonical role of HOE-1 is to cleave 3'-trailer sequences from nascent tRNAs (Nashimoto et al., 1999; Mayer et al., 2000; Schiffer et al., 2002; Takaku et al., 2003; Dubrovsky et al., 2004; Brzezniak et al., 2011; Sanchez et al., 2011; Siira et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The enzymatic function of HOE-1 is dependent upon zinc binding.
source: This enzymatic function is dependent upon zinc binding (Ma et al., 2017; Bienert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Animals homozygous for D624A recapitulate the growth arrest phenotype of the hoe-1 null mutant.
source: Animals homozygous for D624A recapitulate the growth arrest phenotype of the hoe-1 null mutant precluding us from assessing the impact of D624A on UPRmt induction in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental characterization of the mutant.

claim: A single copy of catalytically dead hoe-1 is sufficient to attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: A single copy of catalytically dead hoe-1 is sufficient to attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt requires the catalytic activity of HOE-1.
source: These data suggest that hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt requires the catalytic activity of HOE-1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that a catalytically dead version attenuates UPRmt.

claim: Production of mature tRNAs begins with transcription of tRNA gene loci by RNA polymerase III.
source: Production of mature tRNAs begins with transcription of tRNA gene loci by RNA polymerase III followed by sequential cleavage of 5'-leader and 3'-trailer sequences from immature tRNA transcripts by RNase P and HOE-1, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of tRNA biogenesis.

claim: Mature tRNA production involves sequential cleavage of 5'-leader and 3'-trailer sequences from immature tRNA transcripts by RNase P and HOE-1, respectively.
source: Production of mature tRNAs begins with transcription of tRNA gene loci by RNA polymerase III followed by sequential cleavage of 5'-leader and 3'-trailer sequences from immature tRNA transcripts by RNase P and HOE-1, respectively.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of tRNA biogenesis.

claim: Following cleavage of 3'-trailer sequences, tRNAs can be transported to the cytosol by tRNA exportin.
source: Following cleavage of 3'-trailer sequences, tRNAs can be transported to the cytosol by tRNA exportin (Hopper and Nostramo, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: rpc-1 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: Indeed, we found that rpc-1 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: rpc-1 RNAi has little impact on mitochondrial stress-induced UPRmt (nuo-6(qm200)).
source: Interestingly, rpc-1 RNAi has little impact on mitochondrial stress-induced UPRmt (nuo-6(qm200)) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: rpc-1 is required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: These data show that rpc-1 is required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt and support our hypothesis that increased 3'-tRNA processing by HOE-1 activates UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that rpc-1 RNAi blocks hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: For the majority of tRNAs 5'-end processing by the RNase P complex is a prerequisite for 3'-end processing by HOE-1.
source: For the majority of tRNAs 5'-end processing by the RNase P complex is a prerequisite for 3'-end processing by HOE-1 (Frendewey et al., 1985; Yoo and Wolin, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: RNAi against popl-1 attenuates UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: RNAi against a subunit of the RNase P complex, popl-1, attenuates UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: popl-1 RNAi attenuates UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200).
source: popl-1 RNAi also attenuates both UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) (Figure 6C and D) as well as basal induction of ges-1p::GFPcyto (Figure 6E and F), albeit to a lesser extent than the attenuation seen in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: popl-1 RNAi attenuates basal induction of ges-1p::GFPcyto.
source: popl-1 RNAi also attenuates both UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) (Figure 6C and D) as well as basal induction of ges-1p::GFPcyto (Figure 6E and F), albeit to a lesser extent than the attenuation seen in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Elevated 3'-tRNA processing in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is responsible for UPRmt activation.
source: These data suggest that popl-1 RNAi may have a broad impact on protein expression but supports that elevated 3'-tRNA processing in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is responsible for UPRmt activation given that popl-1 RNAi strongly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking 5'-end processing attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: xpo-3 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: Strikingly, xpo-3 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt(Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate nuo-6(qm200) induced UPRmt.
source: However, xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate nuo-6(qm200) induced UPRmt (Figure 6I and J) nor basal ges-1p::GFP levels (Figure 6K and L).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate basal ges-1p::GFP levels.
source: However, xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate nuo-6(qm200) induced UPRmt (Figure 6I and J) nor basal ges-1p::GFP levels (Figure 6K and L).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6K and L.

claim: In hoe-1(ΔNES) animals 3'-processed tRNAs are required in the cytosol to activate UPRmt.
source: These data suggest that in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals 3'-processed tRNAs are required in the cytosol to activate UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking tRNA export attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: Knockdown of rtcb-1 mildly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: Knockdown of both tRNA ligase, rtcb-1, and tRNA nucleotidyl transferase, hpo-31 mildly attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Knockdown of hpo-31 mildly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: Knockdown of both tRNA ligase, rtcb-1, and tRNA nucleotidyl transferase, hpo-31 mildly attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: rtcb-1 RNAi mildly attenuates nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt.
source: However, rtcb-1 RNAi also mildly attenuates nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D and E.

claim: tRNA ligation and CCA addition have limited involvement in hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: These data suggest that tRNA ligation and CCA addition have limited involvement in hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from the mild effects of rtcb-1 and hpo-31 RNAi on hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: UPRmt induction by nuclear export deficient HOE-1 is the result of increased 3'-tRNA processing.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that UPRmt induction by nuclear export deficient HOE-1 is the result of increased 3'-tRNA processing and that these tRNA species are required in the cytosol to trigger UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing requirement for tRNA processing and export.

claim: tRNA species processed by HOE-1 are required in the cytosol to trigger UPRmt.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that UPRmt induction by nuclear export deficient HOE-1 is the result of increased 3'-tRNA processing and that these tRNA species are required in the cytosol to trigger UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for tRNA export (xpo-3) for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: Uncharged tRNAs activate the kinase GCN2 in the integrated stress response (ISR).
source: One such pathway is the integrated stress response (ISR) in which uncharged tRNAs activate the kinase GCN2 which, in turn, phosphorylates the eukaryotic translation initiation factor, eIF2α.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ISR pathway.

claim: GCN2 phosphorylates the eukaryotic translation initiation factor, eIF2α.
source: One such pathway is the integrated stress response (ISR) in which uncharged tRNAs activate the kinase GCN2 which, in turn, phosphorylates the eukaryotic translation initiation factor, eIF2α.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ISR pathway.

claim: Inhibitory phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to upregulation of the transcription factor ATF4.
source: This inhibitory phosphorylation of eIF2α leads to upregulation of a select number of proteins including the transcription factor ATF4 (Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016; Costa-Mattioli and Walter, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ATF4 and ATF5 are orthologs of ATFS-1.
source: Interestingly, ATF4 and one of its targets, ATF5, are orthologs of ATFS-1 (Fiorese et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: GCN2 and ISR have been shown to be responsive to mitochondrial stress.
source: Moreover, GCN2 and ISR in general have been shown to be responsive to mitochondrial stress (Baker et al., 2012; Fessler et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2020; Koncha et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only slightly reduced in a gcn-2 null background.
source: We found that hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only slightly reduced in both a gcn-2 null (gcn-2(ok871)) and an eIF2α non-phosphorylatable mutant (eIF2α(S46A,S49A)) background (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only slightly reduced in an eIF2α non-phosphorylatable mutant background.
source: We found that hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only slightly reduced in both a gcn-2 null (gcn-2(ok871)) and an eIF2α non-phosphorylatable mutant (eIF2α(S46A,S49A)) background (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: A mechanism independent of ISR is largely responsible for UPRmt activation by hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: These data suggest that a mechanism independent of ISR must largely be responsible for UPRmt activation by hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking ISR has minimal effect on hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: Both primer pairs for hoe-1 mRNA measured similar levels of hoe-1 mRNA.
source: However, we found that both primer pairs measured similar levels of hoe-1 mRNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) suggesting that, like in other systems, there is a single hoe-1 transcript.
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a single hoe-1 transcript in C. elegans.
source: However, we found that both primer pairs measured similar levels of hoe-1 mRNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) suggesting that, like in other systems, there is a single hoe-1 transcript.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both primer pairs detect similar mRNA levels.

claim: hoe-1 mRNA levels are modestly elevated in nuo-6(qm200) animals relative to wildtype.
source: We found, using both primer pairs, that hoe-1 mRNA levels are modestly elevated in nuo-6(qm200) animals relative to wildtype (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C) suggesting that hoe-1 may be transcriptionally upregulated under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: hoe-1 may be transcriptionally upregulated under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
source: We found, using both primer pairs, that hoe-1 mRNA levels are modestly elevated in nuo-6(qm200) animals relative to wildtype (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and C) suggesting that hoe-1 may be transcriptionally upregulated under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of elevated hoe-1 mRNA in mitochondrial stress conditions.

claim: HOE-1::GFP nuclear levels are markedly diminished under mitochondrial stress induced by nuo-6(qm200), cco-1 RNAi, and spg-7 RNAi.
source: We found that HOE-1::GFP nuclear levels are markedly diminished under mitochondrial stress induced by nuo-6(qm200), cco-1 RNAi, and spg-7 RNAi (Figure 8A and B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 8A and B and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: HOE-1 levels are significantly upregulated in nuclei of nuo-6(qm200) animals on atfs-1 RNAi relative to nuo-6(qm200) animals on control RNAi.
source: HOE-1 levels are significantly upregulated in nuclei of nuo-6(qm200) animals on atfs-1 RNAi relative to nuo-6(qm200) animals on control RNAi, as well as both wildtype animals on control and atfs-1 RNAi (Figure 8A and B and Figure 8—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 8A and B and Figure 8—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Total cellular HOE-1 levels are elevated under mitochondrial stress in an atfs-1 RNAi background.
source: Moreover, total cellular HOE-1 levels are elevated under mitochondrial stress in an atfs-1 RNAi background (Figure 8C and D and Figure 8—source data 1A–E and Figure 8—source data 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claim: Mitochondrial HOE-1 levels are elevated under mitochondrial stress conditions irrespective of RNAi treatment.
source: Additionally, mitochondrial HOE-1 levels are elevated under mitochondrial stress conditions irrespective of RNAi treatment (Figure 8—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3D.

claim: HOE-1 is upregulated and accumulates in nuclei upon mitochondrial stress.
source: Together these data suggest that HOE-1 is upregulated and accumulates in nuclei upon mitochondrial stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking UPRmt reveals elevated nuclear HOE-1 under stress.

claim: Nuclear HOE-1 is negatively regulated by ATFS-1 once UPRmt is activated.
source: Then, nuclear HOE-1 is negatively regulated by ATFS-1 once UPRmt is activated.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that atfs-1 RNAi increases nuclear HOE-1 under stress conditions.

claim: Nuclear HOE-1 levels are markedly reduced in atfs-1(et15) animals relative to wildtype.
source: Indeed, nuclear HOE-1 levels are markedly reduced in atfs-1(et15) animals relative to wildtype (Figure 8E and F and Figure 8—figure supplement 4A–C)
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 8E and F and Figure 8—figure supplement 4A-C.

claim: Total and mitochondrial HOE-1 protein levels are largely unperturbed in atfs-1(et15) animals.
source: while total and mitochondrial HOE-1 protein levels are largely unperturbed (Figure 8G and H, Figure 8—figure supplement 4D, Figure 8—source data 3A–E and Figure 8—source data 4A–E).
evidence: Supported by western blot and confocal imaging data shown in Figure 8G and H and Figure 8—figure supplement 4D.

claim: UPRmt activation negatively regulates nuclear HOE-1.
source: These data further support that UPRmt activation negatively regulates nuclear HOE-1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that constitutive UPRmt activation reduces nuclear HOE-1.

claim: Multiple factors have been identified that are required for maximal activation of UPRmt.
source: Multiple factors have been identified that are required for maximal activation of UPRmt.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: CLPP-1 protease is required for maximal activation of UPRmt.
source: This includes the mitochondrial localized proteins, CLPP-1 protease and peptide transmembrane transporter HAF-1 (Haynes et al., 2007; Haynes et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: HAF-1 is required for maximal activation of UPRmt.
source: This includes the mitochondrial localized proteins, CLPP-1 protease and peptide transmembrane transporter HAF-1 (Haynes et al., 2007; Haynes et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1 are required for UPRmt activation.
source: Additionally, the transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1 along with the co-transcriptional activator UBL-5 are required for UPRmt activation (Benedetti et al., 2006; Haynes et al., 2007; Haynes et al., 2010; Nargund et al., 2012; Nargund et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The co-transcriptional activator UBL-5 is required for UPRmt activation.
source: Additionally, the transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1 along with the co-transcriptional activator UBL-5 are required for UPRmt activation (Benedetti et al., 2006; Haynes et al., 2007; Haynes et al., 2010; Nargund et al., 2012; Nargund et al., 2015; Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Histone modifications are involved in fully activating UPRmt.
source: Histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and post-translational modifications of ATFS-1 are also involved in fully activating UPRmt (Tian et al., 2016; Merkwirth et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Chromatin remodeling is involved in fully activating UPRmt.
source: Histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and post-translational modifications of ATFS-1 are also involved in fully activating UPRmt (Tian et al., 2016; Merkwirth et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Post-translational modifications of ATFS-1 are involved in fully activating UPRmt.
source: Histone modifications, chromatin remodeling, and post-translational modifications of ATFS-1 are also involved in fully activating UPRmt (Tian et al., 2016; Merkwirth et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2019; Shao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Nuclear HOE-1 is required for maximal activation of UPRmt.
source: We show for the first time that nuclear HOE-1 is required for maximal activation of UPRmt as its induction by various stressors is attenuated in hoe-1 RNAi, hoe-1 null, and hoe-1(ΔNLS) backgrounds.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing attenuation of UPRmt in various hoe-1 loss-of-function conditions.

claim: Loss of hoe-1 results in varied attenuation of UPRmt depending on how UPRmt is activated.
source: We show that loss of hoe-1 results in varied attenuation of UPRmt depending on how UPRmt is activated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing different degrees of attenuation with different stressors.

claim: UPRmt induction by RNAi (cco-1 and spg-7) is robustly attenuated by loss of hoe-1.
source: UPRmt induction by RNAi (cco-1 and spg-7) is robustly attenuated by loss of hoe-1 while nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt is only modestly attenuated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt is only modestly attenuated by loss of hoe-1.
source: UPRmt induction by RNAi (cco-1 and spg-7) is robustly attenuated by loss of hoe-1 while nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt is only modestly attenuated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: RNAi by feeding works well in all tissues except neurons.
source: RNAi by feeding works well in all tissues except neurons (Timmons et al., 2001; Kamath et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: UPRmt can be activated non-cell autonomously in the intestine by mitochondrial stress in neurons.
source: Importantly, UPRmt can be activated non-cell autonomously in the intestine by mitochondrial stress in neurons (Durieux et al., 2011; Berendzen et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: UPRmt induced cell-autonomously in the intestine by RNAi may be hoe-1 dependent.
source: UPRmt induced cell-autonomously in the intestine by RNAi may be hoe-1 dependent while neuron-to-intestine UPRmt induction may work primarily in a hoe-1-independent manner.
evidence: Speculated based on the differential effects of hoe-1 loss on different UPRmt induction methods.

claim: Neuron-to-intestine UPRmt induction may work primarily in a hoe-1-independent manner.
source: UPRmt induced cell-autonomously in the intestine by RNAi may be hoe-1 dependent while neuron-to-intestine UPRmt induction may work primarily in a hoe-1-independent manner.
evidence: Speculated based on the differential effects of hoe-1 loss on different UPRmt induction methods.

claim: Increased nuclear accumulation of HOE-1 only activates UPRmt in the intestine.
source: Consistent with this, increased nuclear accumulation of HOE-1 only activates UPRmt in the intestine.
evidence: Supported by tissue-specific degradation experiments.

claim: UPRmt is generally triggered via compromised mitochondrial membrane potential which facilitates the nuclear accumulation of ATFS-1.
source: UPRmt is generally triggered via compromised mitochondrial membrane potential which facilitates the nuclear accumulation of ATFS-1 (Rolland et al., 2019; Shpilka et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: UPRmt activation via hoe-1(ΔNES) correlates with a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: We find that UPRmt activation via hoe-1(ΔNES) correlates with a decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential providing a potential trigger for UPRmt induction.
evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data.

claim: The UPRmt transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1 have increased nuclear localization in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: Furthermore, we show that the UPRmt transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1 have increased nuclear localization in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals, thus likely facilitating the robust UPRmt activation.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data.

claim: Increased 3'-tRNA processing by HOE-1 is likely responsible for UPRmt activation.
source: Here, we show that increased 3'-tRNA processing by HOE-1 is likely responsible for UPRmt activation.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing requirement for tRNA processing enzymes and export.

claim: Restricting HOE-1-dependent 3'-tRNA trailer sequence cleavage indirectly by RNAi against rpc-1 strongly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: Restricting HOE-1-dependent 3'-tRNA trailer sequence cleavage indirectly by RNAi against RNA polymerase III subunit, rpc-1, and RNase P subunit, popl-1, strongly attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Restricting HOE-1-dependent 3'-tRNA trailer sequence cleavage indirectly by RNAi against popl-1 strongly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
source: Restricting HOE-1-dependent 3'-tRNA trailer sequence cleavage indirectly by RNAi against RNA polymerase III subunit, rpc-1, and RNase P subunit, popl-1, strongly attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: RNA species processed by HOE-1 must be required in the cytosol to activate UPRmt.
source: Moreover, these RNA species must be required in the cytosol to activate UPRmt as RNAi against tRNA exportin xpo-3 is sufficient to robustly attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking tRNA export attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: The findings are the first reported connection between altered tRNA processing and UPRmt in C. elegans.
source: Our findings herein are the first reported connection between altered tRNA processing and UPRmt in C. elegans.
evidence: Stated as a novel finding of this study.

claim: tRNAs have emerged as small RNAs with important regulatory roles inside cells.
source: However, besides performing their core housekeeping function in protein translation, tRNAs have also emerged as small RNAs with important regulatory roles inside cells (Avcilar-Kucukgoze and Kashina, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: The most well-characterized regulatory role for tRNAs is in the activation of the integrated stress response (ISR).
source: Perhaps, the most well-characterized regulatory role for tRNAs is in the activation of the integrated stress response (ISR).
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: gcn-2 and eIF2α are not required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt activation.
source: However, we show that gcn-2 and eIF2α are not required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt activation suggesting that a different mechanism is responsible.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The lack of involvement of ISR in HOE-1's role in UPRmt is not too surprising as there may be a greater pool of fully mature tRNAs in the cytosol in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: The lack of involvement of ISR in HOE-1's role in UPRmt is not too surprising as there may be a greater pool of fully mature tRNAs in the cytosol in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals due to increased 3'-end processing of tRNAs above wildtype levels.
evidence: Speculated based on the mechanism of HOE-1 action.

claim: Increased 3'-end processing of tRNAs in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals would result in an excess of charged tRNAs in the cytosol.
source: This would result in an excess of charged tRNAs in the cytosol, the opposite of what is required to trigger GCN2-dependent ISR.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of tRNA processing and ISR activation.

claim: The use of amino acids to charge excess tRNAs in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals may limit the pool of free amino acids available for mitochondrial import.
source: For example, the use of amino acids to charge excess tRNAs in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals may limit the pool of free amino acids available for mitochondrial import, thus affecting translation of proteins encoded by the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: Speculated as a possible mechanism for UPRmt activation.

claim: Limiting free amino acids for mitochondrial import may affect translation of proteins encoded by the mitochondrial genome.
source: For example, the use of amino acids to charge excess tRNAs in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals may limit the pool of free amino acids available for mitochondrial import, thus affecting translation of proteins encoded by the mitochondrial genome.
evidence: Speculated as a possible mechanism for UPRmt activation.

claim: Stoichiometric imbalance between nuclear and mitochondrial-encoded components of the electron transport chain is known to compromise mitochondrial membrane potential and trigger UPRmt.
source: This may result in stoichiometric imbalance between nuclear and mitochondrial-encoded components of the electron transport chain, which is known to compromise mitochondrial membrane potential and trigger UPRmt (Houtkooper et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: Mito-nuclear imbalance in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals may result from excessive translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins due to increased abundance of available charged tRNAs in the cytosol.
source: Alternatively, mito-nuclear imbalance in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals may result from excessive translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins due to increased abundance of available charged tRNAs in the cytosol.
evidence: Speculated as an alternative mechanism for UPRmt activation.

claim: UPRmt may be due to changes in the levels of specific tRNAs that preferentially impact translation of genes enriched for the corresponding codons.
source: In yet another scenario, UPRmt may not be the consequence of a global increase in the levels of all cytosolic tRNAs but rather, may be due to changes in the levels of specific tRNAs that preferentially impact translation of genes enriched for the corresponding codons.
evidence: Speculated as another possible mechanism for UPRmt activation.

claim: Selective upregulation of tRNAs has been shown previously to have specific cellular consequences.
source: Such selective upregulation of tRNAs has been shown previously to have specific cellular consequences (Gingold et al., 2014; Goodarzi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: A tRNA-like RNA or other small RNA species such as tRNA fragments may be responsible for UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
source: Finally, it is possible that a tRNA-like RNA or other small RNA species such as tRNA fragments are responsible for UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Kruszka et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2009; Bogerd et al., 2010; Siira et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculated as another possible mechanism for UPRmt activation.

claim: If a tRNA-like RNA or tRNA fragment is responsible for UPRmt induction, such an RNA species would need to be transported to the cytosol by tRNA exportin.
source: However, if this is the case, our data argue that such an RNA species would need to be transported to the cytosol by tRNA exportin.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement for xpo-3 for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claim: Non-tRNA transport by an ortholog of xpo-3 has not yet been reported.
source: Non-tRNA transport by an ortholog of xpo-3 has not yet been reported (Hopper and Nostramo, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claim: Nuclear HOE-1 is dynamically regulated by mitochondrial stress.
source: We show that nuclear HOE-1 is dynamically regulated by mitochondrial stress.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data showing changes in nuclear HOE-1 levels under stress.

claim: In the presence of mitochondrial stress, nuclear HOE-1 levels are depleted.
source: In the presence of stress, nuclear HOE-1 levels are depleted.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data.

claim: HOE-1 nuclear levels under mitochondrial stress are elevated above wild-type levels when UPRmt is blocked by atfs-1 RNAi.
source: However, this is UPRmt dependent as HOE-1 nuclear levels under mitochondrial stress are elevated above wild-type levels when UPRmt is blocked by atfs-1 RNAi.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data.

claim: Upon mitochondrial stress, nuclear HOE-1 levels are elevated, which elevates 3'-tRNA processing thereby triggering a signaling cascade that results in elevated nuclear ATFS-1 and DVE-1 and subsequent UPRmt induction.
source: These data, paired with the fact that compromising HOE-1 nuclear export triggers UPRmt, lead us to hypothesize that upon mitochondrial stress, nuclear HOE-1 levels are elevated. This upregulation of nuclear HOE-1 elevates 3'-tRNA processing thereby triggering a signaling cascade that results in elevated nuclear ATFS-1 and DVE-1 and subsequent UPRmt induction.
evidence: Hypothesized based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Activated UPRmt negatively regulates HOE-1 nuclear levels thus providing a feedback mechanism to tightly control mitochondrial stress response.
source: Activated UPRmt then negatively regulates HOE-1 nuclear levels thus providing a feedback mechanism to tightly control mitochondrial stress response.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that UPRmt activation reduces nuclear HOE-1.

claim: UPRmt-negative regulation of HOE-1 is further supported by data showing that constitutive activation of UPRmt by atfs-1(et15) is sufficient to reduce nuclear HOE-1 levels in the absence of mitochondrial stress.
source: UPRmt-negative regulation of HOE-1 is further supported by our data showing that constitutive activation of UPRmt by atfs-1(et15) is sufficient to reduce nuclear HOE-1 levels in the absence of mitochondrial stress.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data.

claim: Multiple mitochondrial derived small molecules have been reported to communicate mitochondrial status including reactive oxygen species (ROS), NAD+, and acetyl-CoA.
source: Multiple mitochondrial derived small molecules have been reported to communicate mitochondrial status including reactive oxygen species (ROS), NAD+, and acetyl-CoA (Baker et al., 2012; Mouchiroud et al., 2013; Ramachandran et al., 2019; Tjahjono et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mutations in ELAC2 are associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in humans.
source: In humans, mutations in the ortholog of HOE-1, ELAC2, are associated with both hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Haack et al., 2013; Shinwari et al., 2017; Saoura et al., 2019) and prostate cancer (Tavtigian et al., 2001; Korver et al., 2003; Noda et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mutations in ELAC2 are associated with prostate cancer in humans.
source: In humans, mutations in the ortholog of HOE-1, ELAC2, are associated with both hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Haack et al., 2013; Shinwari et al., 2017; Saoura et al., 2019) and prostate cancer (Tavtigian et al., 2001; Korver et al., 2003; Noda et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: It has been suggested that mutations in ELAC2 cause disease because of a loss of mature tRNA production.
source: Historically, it has been suggested that mutations in ELAC2 cause disease because of a loss of mature tRNA production.
evidence: Based on established hypotheses in the field.

claim: ELAC2 mutations may lead to altered tRNA processing that triggers aberrant stress response signaling resulting in disease state.
source: Our works suggests an intriguing alternative whereby ELAC2 mutations lead to altered tRNA processing that triggers aberrant stress response signaling resulting in disease state.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings of this study.

claim: The C. elegans system provides a convenient opportunity to interrogate disease causing variants of ELAC2.
source: Our system provides a convenient opportunity to interrogate these disease causing variants.
evidence: Stated as a potential application of this study.

claim: The findings provide a novel mechanism—involving the tRNA processing enzyme HOE-1—by which mitochondrial stress is transduced to activate UPRmt.
source: Taken together, our findings provide a novel mechanism—involving the tRNA processing enzyme HOE-1—by which mitochondrial stress is transduced to activate UPRmt thus providing important insight into the regulation of mitochondrial stress response.
evidence: Summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: The findings provide important insight into the regulation of mitochondrial stress response.
source: Taken together, our findings provide a novel mechanism—involving the tRNA processing enzyme HOE-1—by which mitochondrial stress is transduced to activate UPRmt thus providing important insight into the regulation of mitochondrial stress response.
evidence: Summarizes the significance of the study.
